Items.Authors: Edwin Fernando Cruz Aguirre, Keri Hoadley, Jessica S. Li, Greyson Davis, Allison Youngblood
Items.Title: CRAFTS: an extreme ultraviolet sounding rocket mission concept
Items.Abstract: The Coronal Radiation of Active F-Type Stars (CRAFTS) sounding rocket is designed to observe the extreme ultraviolet (EUV) radiation environments of nearby, active F-type stars identified as priority targets for the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO). Stellar EUV emission drives exoplanet atmospheric escape; CRAFTS aims to determine if F-type stars are suitable targets for HWO. The telescope consists of two off-axis parabolic mirrors, split from a 400 mm on-axis paraboloid. Custom multi-layer (ML) coatings on each half define the EUV1 (16.5 – 21.5 nm), and EUV2 (24.5 – 29.5 nm) bands. The halves are radially offset, producing separate images onto a CCD detector. An aluminum filter rejects out-of-band light. High EUV sensitivity is achieved through a prime focus design, high-reflectivity ML coatings, and an aluminum filter, either standalone or directly coated onto the detector. The peak effective areas of EUV1 and EUV2 are ~70 cm2 and ~58 cm2, respectively.

Items.Authors: Douglas Jordan
Items.Title: Digital CMOS image sensors for astronomy from Teledyne: A comparison to CCDs
Items.Abstract: As detectors for astronomy become more complex their capabilities increase but also make the selection of the best detector for a given application more difficult. This paper attempts to describe the main differences as well as the advantages and disadvantages of different detector types. A comparison between Teledyne e2v's CCDs for astronomy, such as the CCD290-99, and the new generation of CMOS detectors, such as the CIS303 and CIS304, will be presented, looking back at previous projects and forwards to projects both current and proposed.  The back-thinning and application of anti-reflection coatings on imaging sensors are also key to their performance, this paper will also detail new developments and results for this key part of the manufacturing process.

Items.Authors: Keri Hoadley, Curtis McCully, Fernando Cruz Aguirre, Gillian Kyne, Greyson Davis, Jessica S. Li, Moira Andrews, Azalee Bostroem, Peter J. Brown, Erika T. Hamden, Daniel R. Harbeck, John J. Hennessy, Michael E. Hoenk, Griffin Hosseinzadeh, D. Andrew Howell, April D. Jewell, Peter Milne, Leonidas A. Moustakas, Shouleh Nikzad, Abigail Polin, David J. Sand, Ken J. Shen, Lisa J. Storrie-Lombardi, Craig Pellegrino, Daichi Hiramatsu
Items.Title: The Ultraviolet Type Ia supernova (UVIa) mission concept: from CubeSat to SmallSat and beyond
Items.Abstract: UVIa is SmallSat mission concept, comprised of an Ultraviolet (UV) and Optical imaging telescope, that simultaneously stands to resolve long-standing questions about the explosion mechanisms of Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) and constraining the equation of state of dark energy for cosmology. UVIa acts as a rapid, reactive observatory that will trigger on newly discovered Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) with simultaneous optical (u-band), near-ultraviolet (NUV: 200-240nm), and far-ultraviolet (FUV: 160-180nm) imaging. UVIa is designed to accomplish two key science objectives: 1) to determine the explosion physics of SNe Ia by uncovering their progenitors, and 2) to provide templates of temporal UV photometry for nearby SNe Ia to calibrate intermediate redshift SNe Ia discovered by next-generation optical/infrared observatories. UVIa compliments next generation observatories, like UVEX, allowing them to optimize their response and observing cadence on targets of interest.

Items.Authors: Jill Juneau, Christopher Layden, Nathan Lourie, Danielle Frostig, Gustav Pettersson, Bruno Gili, Alberto Villegas, Antonio Sanchez, Gema Valles, Jose Segovia, Elio Angilè, Mark Bautz, Gabor Furesz, Sarah Heine, Beverly LaMarr, Gregory Prigozhin
Items.Title: Assessing low-signal non-linearity improvements in the updated Teledyne COSMOS camera design
Items.Abstract: The first-generation Teledyne COSMOS CMOS camera exhibited an unexpected non-linearity at very low signal levels, impacting its ability for faint object detection in precision astronomy applications. Teledyne has since redesigned the pixel architecture to address this issue. We evaluate this new design using a 4.8k × 4.8k test sensor and repeat the original illumination-ramp experiments that revealed the problem. This work presents the first results from the updated architecture and assesses whether the redesign successfully improves linearity in the faint-signal regime critical for precision astronomy.

Items.Authors: Marc F. Kassis
Items.Title: Innovations and advances in instrumentation at the W. M. Keck Observatory, vol. IV
Items.Abstract: Throughout its three decades of operation, the twin 10-meter W. M. Keck Observatory (WMKO) telescopes have maximized their scientific impact to produce transformative discoveries. Primary technology partners at Caltech and the University of California lead upgrade and facility instrumentation projects yet WMKO has a growing and collaborative partnerships with the University of Notre Dame, the University of Hawaii, Swinburne, and The Netherlands Organization. Guided by the observatory’s strategic plan, our leadership developed a five-year implementation plan that includes major technology developments and new facility class instrumentation that adapts and responds to the evolving science needs and includes phased retirements for existing capabilities. We present the status of observatory infrastructure projects, technology upgrades, and new instrument additions as well as planned instrumentation projects in early and advanced stages of development.

Items.Authors: Michael W. McElwain
Items.Title: The era of large space telescopes: from Webb's revolutionary infrared sensitivity to Roman's wide fields and Habitable World’s quest for another Earth
Items.Abstract: We are in the era of large space telescopes, which will transform our understanding of the cosmos. The ambitious James Webb Space Telescope is making infrared observations with unprecedented sensitivity and has exceeded its performance expectations. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is approaching its launch and science operations, with observational capabilities that will carry out panoramic wide-field infrared surveys. On the horizon, the Habitable Worlds Observatory will directly image Earth-like exoplanets and search their atmospheres for biosignatures. I will describe how each large space telescope mission strategically builds upon the technological foundations of its predecessors, creating synergies to answer some of humanity’s most profound questions. The path from Webb to Roman to HWO illustrates technological progress and an ambitious strategic vision for space astronomy that promises to deliver transformational discoveries for decades to come.

Items.Authors: Laird M. Close, Jialin Li, Jared R. Males, Sebastiaan Haffert, Olivier Guyon, Joseph Long, Alycia Weinberger, Katherine Follette, Joshua Liberman, Katie Twitchell, Jay Kueny, Daniel Apai, Laura Perez, Maggie Kautz, Eden McEwen, Logan Pearce, Kevin Wagner, Gabriel Weible, Rene Doyon
Items.Title: A review of high-contrast detection of accreting proto-planets with visible ExAO at H-alpha: the MagAO-X MaXProtoPlanetS survey results
Items.Abstract: We will review the results of our multi-year program’s direct imaging at H-alpha (656.3 nm) of the young (~5 Myr old) accreting protoplanets PDS 70 b, PDS 70 c, 2MJ1612 b and WISPIT 2b with visible ExAO and the MaxProtoPlanetS survey in general. These are very high-contrast ~10^-5 observations of these planets with separations of 100-300 mas in the visible at H-alpha with the 6.5m Magellan Telescope and the 2040 actuator MagAO-X visible ExAO system. From this, admittedly small, sample of observed protoplanets we can now start to see some general trends newly emerge --which are exciting to explore in this AO science talk. We will review what we have recently learned about the spread of planet masses, accretion rates, H-alpha line fluxes/variability, and protoplanet inclinations. We will briefly highlight the exciting new hardware upgrades to MagAO-X’s H-alpha SDI mode (like the new PIAACMC coronagraph). General lessons learned about doing exciting ExAO at H-alpha will also be shared.

Items.Authors: Aafaque R. Khan, Christopher Carr, Himash Rathore, Maitland Bowen, Nazende Kerkeser, Carlos Vargas, Erika Hamden, Gurtina Besla, Keri Hoadley, David Schiminovich
Items.Title: Mileva: a UV SmallSat constellation for wide-field spectroscopic mapping of the circumgalactic medium in a galaxy interaction
Items.Abstract: Mileva is a proposed ultraviolet SmallSat constellation designed to map faint, diffuse circumgalactic gas in the dynamic Milky Way–Large Magellanic Cloud (MW–LMC) interaction region. Each spacecraft carries a compact R≈1500–3000 UV spectrograph optimised for a single diagnostic line, enabling simultaneous multi-phase mapping of OVI, CIV, SiIII, and MgII emission. The mission design is informed by forward-modelled UV emission maps from hydrodynamical simulations, which drive sensitivity, bandpass, and étendue requirements. We present the instrument and mission trade space, including spectrograph configuration, detector architecture, reflective coatings, and background-limited performance in the 1000–3000 Å band. The constellation architecture increases survey speed and sky coverage while providing cost advantages of replicated instrument design. Mileva demonstrates how coordinated UV SmallSats can enable cost-efficient wide-field spectroscopic surveys of the diffuse universe.

Items.Authors: Peter Verhoeve, Luc Boucher, Ralf Kohley, Conor Robinson, Frederic Lemmel, Erik Ryman, Hans Smit, Sander Blommaert, Malik Mansour, Eloy Hernandez, Thibaut Prod'Homme, Marco Sirianni
Items.Title: First characterisation results of the CIS304-33 detectors for the Arrakihs VIS channels
Items.Abstract: Arrakihs is an ESA fast-class mission designed to probe dark matter and the formation of Milky Way-type galaxies through ultra-deep imaging of faint stellar halos. The mission will test the Lambda-Cold Dark Matter (LCDM) model by providing robust statistics on tidal streams, mapping diffuse halos, and determining satellite galaxy distributions. The two visible channels on Arrakihs use 4.5k x 4.3k CIS304-33 backside illuminated CMOS image sensors from Te2v for imaging in the wavelength range 280-880 nm. This work presents the first results of the electro-optical characterisation of prototype CIS304-33 sensors at ESA. This comprises measurements of noise and gain, dark signal, PRNU, PSF, QE, image lag, cross talk and power consumption in various operating conditions of the detector. These results will support the optimisation of the baseline operating parameters for the Arrakihs VIS channel.

Items.Authors: Jessica A. Gaskin
Items.Title: The ASTRA Initiative: Preparing for future NASA large strategic astrophysics missions
Items.Abstract: This presentation summarizes he Astrophysics Strategic Technology & Research Accelerator (ASTRA) Initiative and discusses, NASA’s progress in executing the Astro2020 Decadal Survey recommendations, and outlines the strategic steps being undertaken to prepare for future strategic astrophysics missions. Support for the community considers previous efforts – including existing concept studies developed for Astro2020, the current global astronomical environment of existing and planned missions, increased industry capability, and technological advances/investments over the past decade. The discussion will highlight the interplay of technological advancements and mission planning essential for future exploration in astrophysics and astronomy and will emphasize the value and criticality of industry and international partnering.

Items.Authors: Joannah L. Hinz, Joseph Shields
Items.Title: Current instrumentation status at the Large Binocular Telescope Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Large Binocular Telescope hosts a large, versatile suite of instruments for use in monocular or binocular modes, including the ability to change configurations during nighttime observing. In addition to the original instrument suite, the LBT now hosts the very high angular resolution SHARK imaging cameras, and commissioning of the new iLocater spectrograph is taking place this year. In May 2025, proposals were accepted for a third generation of instruments at the LBT. These third generation proposals include plans to enhance and upgrade existing capabilities as well as to develop new concepts that will keep the LBT at the forefront of scientific research. We present an overview of our current and future capabilities, the current instrument demand from our member institutions, and the operational transition being made in from the four original founding members to a new consortium.

Items.Authors: Alan Ochoa, Brian Fleming, Amanda Hendrix, Dmitry Vorobiev, Briana Indahl, Rebecca N. Schindhelm
Items.Title: Motivating a reconfigurable UV spectrograph for planetary observations: UMIS concept and prototype progress
Items.Abstract: The ultraviolet reveals rapidly evolving planetary processes including plumes, transient atmospheres, auroral emissions, and exosphere interactions. Long-slit spectrographs have enabled major discoveries, but their one-dimensional sampling limits efficiency for targets that change quickly or span extended regions. The Ultraviolet Micromirror Imaging Spectrograph (UMIS) addresses this by introducing ultraviolet integral-field spectroscopy to planetary science. UMIS replaces the fixed slit with a reconfigurable micromirror array that acts as a programmable pseudo-slit, enabling simultaneous acquisition of hundreds of spectra across a wide field of view while preserving undirected light for contextual UV imaging. The micromirror array from Bright Silicon Technologies features 20 × 20 individually controllable elements that route light to different gratings. We present the planetary science motivations for UMIS and initial results from characterization of a 48-element loaner device.

Items.Authors: Maria Tantalo, Giuliana Fiorentino, Laura Schreiber, Giuseppe Bono, Antonino Nunnari, Emiliano Diolaiti, Davide Ricci, Carmela Lardo, Claudia Mignone, Andrea La Camera, Marcello Ravenna, Vittorio Francesco Braga
Items.Title: Globular clusters as diagnostic to verify adaptive optics performance
Items.Abstract: We present the current stage of the analysis of a sample of Milky Way globular clusters (GCs) observed with AO-assisted telescopes. Their Color-Magnitude Diagrams (CMDs), in particular the dispersion of the evolutionary sequences, are optimal and useful diagnostics to quantitatively measure the quality of the photometry obtained from AO-corrected images. We aim at collecting accurate and precise photometry of GCs in the Milky Way, in order to constrain their absolute ages by identifying a specific feature on the CMDs, namely the main sequence knee (MSK). Near-Infrared (NIR) AO-corrected data are deep enough to allow this kind of measurements. We use the Starfinder code to perform the photometry since one of its main assets is the handling of complex and spatially variable PSFs, typical of AO-corrected images.

Items.Authors: Justin P. Gallagher, Edwin Alexani, Scott Adler, Don F. Figer
Items.Title: Single-Photon Sensing CMOS Detectors for the Habitable Worlds Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) is NASA’s next New Great Observatory concept and the first telescope designed explicitly to search for signs of life on Earth-like exoplanets. Achieving this goal will require exceptionally stable instruments and detectors capable of sensing individual photons in a radiation-rich space environment. While no existing detector technology fully meets HWO’s demanding performance requirements, single-photon sensing CMOS detectors (SPSCMOS) already satisfy several Technology Readiness Level 5 (TRL-5) criteria and are strong candidates for further development.  We present characterization results from multiple Fairchild Imaging HWK4123 SPSCMOS detectors that demonstrate their potential for photon-starved UV/O/IR astrophysics applications. We conclude with a roadmap identifying key improvements needed to mature this technology for HWO.

Items.Authors: Eliad Peretz, Peter Plavchan
Items.Title: The Landolt mission
Items.Abstract: The Landolt mission is NASA’s first dedicated on-orbit stellar calibration observatory, designed to establish SI-traceable photometric standards for ground- and space-based astronomy. Landolt uses a thermally stable payload "star", NIST-calibrated photodiodes, and an onboard reference light system to measure bright stellar standards above the atmosphere, improving on the dominant source of uncertainty in absolute flux calibration. The mission provides a new celestial flux ladder supporting cosmology, exoplanet transit measurements, and survey uniformity for facilities such as Rubin, Roman, Keck, and JWST. This presentation will describe the mission architecture, calibration chain, contamination-control design, payload development status, and the expected accuracy improvements, along with connections to recent hybrid optical-calibration demonstrations, including ORKID and the LCRD–ORCAS–Keck experiment. Will be presented on behalf of the Landolt Mission Team

Items.Authors: Saavidra Perera, Alexander Chaushev, Elinor Gates
Items.Title: using adaptive optics for high-precision transit photometry
Items.Abstract: Transiting exoplanets make up the majority of known exoplanet systems, providing invaluable insights into planetary demographics and compositions. Photometric follow-up is crucial for confirming exoplanet candidates, refining orbital and physical parameters, and enabling atmospheric characterization. However, achieving high photometric precision from the ground remains challenging. For bright targets, the limitation is atmospheric scintillation (i.e. intensity fluctuations). While moving to a larger telescope reduces the effect of scintillation, it still remains the limiting factor relative to photon noise. We propose a method that leverages adaptive optics (AO) wavefront sensing data to measure and mitigate scintillation effects to achieve sub-mmag precision for bright stars (V < 10) from the ground. We present simulated performance and initial on-sky results demonstrating the feasibility and advantages of this approach.

Items.Authors: Kai Zhang, Jean-Louis Lizon, Sharon Xuesong Wang, Wei Xing
Items.Title: CHORUS overview and status
Items.Abstract: CHORUS (Canary Hybrid Optical high-Resolution Ultra-stable Spectrograph) is a powerful science instrument under development for the 10.4m Gran Telescopio Canarias (GTC) in La Palma. This instrument project was jointly proposed by the National Astronomical Observatories of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias (IAC), Nanjing Institute of Astronomical Optics and Technology (NIAOT), and GTC (GRANTECAN S. A.) under the cooperative framework in astronomy between China and Spain, and was kicked off in 2022 with the funding support by the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) . The CHORUS aims to detect and study habitable exoplanets by extremely precision radial velocity measurement and extend the scientific research in some forefront areas such as galactic archeology, black holes, etc., for the decade to come. To reach this scientific goal, this spectrograph provides a spectral resolution of R≥120,000 in the visible wavelength region (420nm–780nm) and R≥25

Items.Authors: Jens Kammerer, Sylvestre Lacour, Mathias Nowak, Jean-Baptiste LeBouquin, Julien Woillez, Sydney Vach, Nicolas Pourré
Items.Title: Boosting exoplanet detection with VLTI/GRAVITY+ using dark hole techniques
Items.Abstract: In this talk, we will provide an overview of our new dark hole operational procedure for high-contrast observations with GRAVITY+. By using a modulation injected with the deformable mirrors of the four GPAO systems, we can constrain the complex electric field at each Unit Telescope (UT) and apply a reference wavefront command which minimizes the residual stellar flux at the position of the science fiber in dual-field mode. This in turn amplifies the signal-to-noise ratio for the faint companion observed with the science fiber, delivering a better contrast performance especially at the smallest angular separations, where the coherent flux in the science fiber is dominated by residual host star flux. We will provide an estimate of the contrast performance gain as a function of the angular separation between the science fiber and the host star (fringe tracking target). Going forward, the dark hole will enable the detection of young giant planets at shorter separations.

Items.Authors: Jonathan Crass, Marshall Johnson, Marcelo Tala Pinto, Michael Engelman, Daniel Pappalardo, Brian Sands, Mark Derwent, Julia Brady, Mark Smithwright, Sai Vidyud Senthil Nathan, Jackson Datkuliak, Christian Schwab, Julian Stürmer, James Smous, Justin R. Crepp, Andrew Bechter, Eric Bechter, David Aikens, Chad Bender, Chris Brandon, Cynthia Brooks, Matheus J. Castro, Jeffrey Chilcote, Al Conrad, Gregory Delo, Peter DeMars, Erin Duell, Matthew Engstrom, Steve Ertel, Louis Fantano, John Keith Feggans, Scott Gaudi, Randy Hamper, Robert Harris, Patrick Hartley, Hali Jackman-Flores, David King, Ondrej Kitzler, Kaitlin Kratter, Jeffrey Kruk, Thomas Legero, Xavier Lesley, Stanimir Letchev, Jerry Mason, Joaquin Mason, Laddawan Miko, Matthew Misch, Jacob Pember, Richard Pogge, Andreas Quirrenbach, Allie Renshaw, Austin Richie, Alexa Rizika, Nandini Sadagopan, Joshua Schlieder, Joseph Shields, Jonathan Shover, Jayde Spiegel, Sahil Sura, Robert Switzer, Joe Thomes, Michael Vansickle, Augustyn Waczynski, Ji Wang, Lauren Weiss, Daniel Wilson, Dane Zielinski-Nicolson
Items.Title: iLocater at the LBT
Items.Abstract: iLocater is a near-infrared, extreme precision radial velocity (EPRV) spectrograph which is being delivered to the dual 8.4m diameter Large Binocular Telescope (LBT) in Spring 2026. The instrument uses single-mode fibers (SMFs) injected with adaptive optics for illumination and is optimized for studies of late-type stars, exoplanet studies, and characterization of stellar variability. We present a status update for the spectrograph and cryostat systems, laboratory characterization, and initial results from the instrument at the LBT.

Items.Authors: José Antonio Rodríguez Losada, Fernando Merlos García, Jorge Quintero Nehrkorn, Víctor Rodríguez Herreros, Camilo Eduardo Jiménez Ángel, Alfonso Cardell Bilbao, Juan José Fernández Valdivia
Items.Title: A multi-middleware integration framework for enabling interoperability between long-lifecycle telescope control systems
Items.Abstract: The 10.4-m Gran Telescopio Canarias (GTC) began science operations in 2009 and is controlled by a distributed system based on RT-CORBA, that complicates long-term maintenance and interoperability with modern subsystems and with new projects such as the EST and NRT. New telescope control systems increasingly rely on heterogeneous middleware technologies, each optimized for different communication needs, creating the challenge of reusing components without binding architectures to a single transport. We present a multi-middleware integration framework based on Enterprise Integration Patterns that provides a unified, transport-agnostic programming model. Core patterns are mapped to multiple backends through pluggable adapters. A neutral in-memory message model and a hybrid router enable fan-out delivery and dynamic transport selection. This approach enables gradual CORBA migration, real-time and telemetry support, and cross-observatory component reuse for multi-decadal operations.

Items.Authors: Tatjana Porwol, Luxuan Cai, Ralf Steinkopf, Johannes Hartung, Melanie Ulitschka, Markus Unger, Stefan Risse, Jan Kinast, Andreas Tünnermann
Items.Title: A novel approach to minimize mid-spatials by chemical-mechanical polishing of metal optics
Items.Abstract: Ultra-precise metal mirrors are crucial in various opto-mechanical systems for, e.g. astronomy and lithography. Surface errors at different spatial frequencies cause light scattering and aberrations. The manufacturing process combines techniques like diamond turning (DT), magnetorheological finishing (MRF), and chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) to correct shape deviations and smooth surfaces. However, machine vibrations and thermal fluctuations can introduce additional errors that are challenging to mitigate. Surface characterization methods, such as white light and Fizeau interferometry, are used to verify these errors. This paper discusses methods to reduce mid-spatial frequency errors (0.1 mm to 3 mm) by CMP, utilizing electroless Nickel-Phosphorous (NiP) plated Aluminum substrates for enhanced polishing techniques.

Items.Authors: David Adriaanse, Eric Grigel, Nancy Valenzuela, Sunil Golwala, Jon Steen, Colin Simmons, Simon Radford, Jim Hayes, Bill Johnson
Items.Title: Decommissioning the Caltech Submillimeter Observatory (CSO) on Maunakea
Items.Abstract: In the final phase of the Caltech Submillimeter Observatory (CSO) lifecycle, the facility on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi was decommissioned, dismantled, removed, and the site renaturalized. This paper covers the program from concept through permitting/approvals to execution, closeout, and acceptance. Work included controlled deconstruction and heavy rigging in a remote, high-elevation environment; hazardous material identification and abatement; regulated waste characterization, handling, and documentation; and restoration with renaturalization measures and verification of site conditions. On Maunakea, cultural and stewardship requirements for work practices, access, environmental controls, and reporting present a crucial driver on all projects. Lessons learned address safety, predictability, accountability, and key cost/schedule drivers for end-of-life decommissioning of ground-based observatories in remote and sensitive locations.

Items.Authors: John S. Pazder, Patrick Côté, Matthew Taylor, Frederic Zamkotsian, Dmitry Vorobiev, Tyrone Woods, Deborah Lockhorst
Items.Title: Development of an UltraViolet Multi-Object Spectroscopic (UVMOS) capability for space astronomy
Items.Abstract: In spring 2024, NRC Canada funded, through its “Small Teams” program, a 2m$cad, three-year project to mature key technologies to enable an Ultraviolet Multi-Object Spectroscopic (UVMOS) capability for space astronomy. A UVMOS instrument is proposed as part of the CASTOR mission. In the CASTOR studies, three key technologies were identified as in need of development: the UV performance of convex gratings, the UV performance of Digital Mirror Devices, and the characterization of UV detectors. The study is now underway, led by NRC-HAA (Victoria, BC) with contributions from: the Laboratoire d’Astrophysique de Marseille (LAM, Marseille, France) ; Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics (LASP, University of Colorado); JPL/Teledyne-e2v/CSA; University of Manitoba . The program will develop and test prototypes for each of these components, followed by the assembly of a UVMOS spectrometer test bench with the aim to raise the technology readiness level of the UVMOS instrument to TRL6.

Items.Authors: Hao-ran Ma, Wen-qing Qu, Yu Ning, Feng Zeng, Shao-zhen Zhu, Xin Luo, Bao-long Chen, Zhe Geng, Hong-fei Zhang, Jian Wang
Items.Title: Infrared Instrumentation for Astronomical observation: Sky Background Measurements and the Development of H- and K-band Infrared Cameras
Items.Abstract: Over the past decade, infrared astronomy in China has progressed from site characterization and small-aperture demonstrations to the engineering development of medium-aperture near-infrared cameras. To address limitations associated with atmospheric thermal background and water vapor, infrared site testing and instrument deployments have been carried out at Dome A in Antarctica, Daocheng in Sichuan, and Lenghu in Qinghai. We will review the development of infrared astronomical instrumentation in China, with emphasis on three contributions from our team: (1) characterizing the J/H/Ks observing conditions at Dome A through dedicated near-infrared sky-background measurements; (2) developing and field-test an H-band infrared camera in Daocheng; and (3) constructing the K-band mosaic focal-plane instrument for the SYSU 80-cm infrared telescope.

Items.Authors: Trevor O. Foote, Elisa V. Quintana, Jessie L. Dotson, Knicole D. Colón, Thomas Barclay, Pete Supsinskas, Jordan Karburn, Dániel Apai, Christina Louise Hedges, Benjamin V. Rackham, Jason F. Rowe, Emily A. Gilbert
Items.Title: The Pandora SmallSat: post-launch operations and mission update
Items.Abstract: The Pandora SmallSat is a NASA Pioneers mission designed to disentangle stellar activity from planetary atmospheric signatures in transmission spectroscopy observations through simultaneous visible photometry and near-infrared spectroscopy. Pandora’s baseline mission lifetime includes a one-month commissioning period followed by a prime mission period of 12 months for science observations. Herein, we present a comprehensive post-launch mission update, detailing operational performance and current observational strategy. We will also highlight key operational milestones, challenges encountered during commissioning and early science operations, and solutions implemented. This information provides insight into Pandora's on-orbit capabilities for precision multiwavelength observations that enable reliable determination of exoplanet atmosphere compositions.

Items.Authors: Eric A. Lintz, Mike Hyman, Felix Radesi, Jennifer Coniglio, Thomas Hordin, Thomas Olson
Items.Title: Improved half-meter class lightweight mirror fabrication
Items.Abstract: Optimax has successfully implemented a Lean manufacturing cell for half-meter class space optics, achieving regular production with eight-week lead times. This presentation provides an operational overview of the integrated manufacturing approach and shares production data demonstrating consistent quality for space flight applications. Key topics include effective customer-vendor collaboration strategies that reduce lead times and costs through early engagement in requirements, specifications and risk management. Technical advancements will be highlighted, including enhanced HERMES smoothing techniques for improved mid-spatial frequency control, metrology enabling rapid feedback loops, and new Silicon Carbide processing capabilities. Data from recent projects validates the manufacturing cell approach as a scalable solution for growing space optics demands.

Items.Authors: Eloy Hernandez, Sander Blommaert, Luc Boucher, Dennis Breeveld, Gertjan Van Duinkerken, Ralf Kohley, Malik Mansour, Marco Oosthoek, Thibaut Prod'Homme, Marco Sirianni, Hans Smit, Peter Verhoeve, Ivo Visser
Items.Title: Signal integrity and electro-optical performance of the Arrakihs NIR channel using a prototype 1.8 μm H2RG detector at 150 K
Items.Abstract: Arrakihs is an ESA fast-class mission designed to probe dark matter and the formation of Milky Way-type galaxies through ultra-deep imaging of faint stellar halos. The mission will test the Lambda-Cold Dark Matter (LCDM) model by providing robust statistics on tidal streams, mapping diffuse halos, and determining satellite galaxy distributions. This work presents the validation campaign for the NIR channel, using a 1.8 μm cut-off prototype H2RG detector operated at 150 K. The study compares buffered and unbuffered readout configurations, assessing trade-offs in signal integrity, noise performance, and power consumption. The electro-optical characterization includes PTC, linearity, full well capacity, PRNU, IPC, dark current, and persistence. Results will guide the selection of baseline operating parameters for Arrakihs NIR and future missions.

Items.Authors: Markus Schulze, Alexander Steiner
Items.Title: Structure conditions monitoring and predictive maintenance of CTAO’s Medium-Sized Telescopes
Items.Abstract: We present the conditions monitoring system for structure-related engineering data of the medium-sized telescopes of the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO). The system integrates vibration sensors on gears and motors, eddy-current displacement sensors on axes, and 3-axis accelerometers on the optical support structure, complemented by electrical, thermal, and environmental health data of the telescope structure. Designed for high availability, it enables early detection of failures and reconstruction of the telescope state at any time. We outline the data-acquisition concept and the planned data-analysis pipeline for predictive maintenance. For example, our drive system analysis uses spectral fingerprinting of vibrations up to 12 kHz to detect anomalous behavior during defined movements of the telescope. Structural diagnostics are performed via a modal analysis, covering damping and resonant excitations from regular telescope motion, wind excitations, and seismic events.

Items.Authors: Briana L. Indahl, Juan M. Alcala, Stefano Basso, Francesco Borsa, Amal Chandran, Marta M. Civitani, Vincenzo Cotroneo, Néstor Espinoza, Davide Fedele, Brian Fleming, Kevin France, Giancarlo Ghirlanda, Fabien Grisé, Kotish Grover, Eliza Kempton, Tommi T. Koskinen, Nicholas Kruczek, Randall L. McEntaffer, Jake A. McCoy, Yamila Miguel, Brunella Nisini, Giovanni Pareschi, Ignazio F. Pillitteri, Laura Proserpio, Peter C. Schneider, Davide Sisana, Dmitry Vorobiev, David J. Wilson, Allison Youngblood
Items.Title: The MANTIS SmallSat mission: a UV observatory for characterizing the high energy stellar radiation environment of exoplanetary systems
Items.Abstract: The MANTIS (Monitoring Activity of Nearby sTars with uv Imaging and Spectroscopy) SmallSat mission, led by the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics (LASP), aims to characterize the impact of ultraviolet stellar radiation on the chemistry and evolution of exoplanetary atmospheres. MANTIS hosts an ambitious optical design consisting of two co-aligned telescopes capable of simultaneous spectroscopy of three passbands (extreme-ultraviolet (100–800A; EUV), far-ultraviolet (1150–1800A; FUV), and near-ultraviolet through visible(2200–5800A; NUV/VIS)) imaged on two detector systems. MANTIS aims to advance three key EUV technologies for astrophysics: A grazing incidence Hetrick-Bowyer telescope contributed by The Italian National Institute for Astrophysics (INAF), a low-scatter grazing incidence EUV grating, and microchannel plate detector with an EUV sensitive KI photocathode. This proceeding overviews the MANTIS mission concept as well as the instrument and spacecraft design.

Items.Authors: Emily Gilbert, Elisa V. Quintana, Jessie L. Dotson, Knicole D. Colón, Thomas Barclay, Pete Supsinskas, Jordan Karburn, Daniel Apai, Christina Hedges, Benjamin Rackham, Jason Rowe, Trevor Foote
Items.Title: The Pandora SmallSat: target selection and early science
Items.Abstract: Pandora is a NASA Pioneers smallsat designed to separate stellar activity from exoplanet atmospheric signals using combined visible photometry and NIR spectroscopy. During its prime mission, Pandora is observing 10 transits of each of the 20 carefully selected K- and M-dwarf systems, targeting a variety of exoplanets. In addition to the prime mission, Pandora also observes auxiliary targets with a wider range of science cases, filling scheduling gaps between prime targets. We will present the target selection strategy, scheduling approach, early science results, and possible extended-mission opportunities.

Items.Title: VLTI system upgrades: recent engineering progress and future developments
Items.Abstract: Over the past six years, the VLTI has undergone major upgrades, improving stability, sensitivity, and operational reliability, enabling the highest-resolution imaging of stars near the Galactic Center, precise exoplanet astrometry, and the resolution of distant quasars. The GRAVITY instrument provides real-time stabilization through its high-speed Fringe Tracker, which also supports MATISSE via GRA4MAT and can now operate in dual-beam mode, enabling off-axis fringe tracking. As part of GRAVITY+, all Unit Telescopes are equipped with advanced adaptive optics systems, including laser guide star units, significantly enhancing sensitivity and sky coverage. GRAVITY+ will further upgrade the GRAVITY instrument with new fiber-coupler mirrors and a high-spectral-resolution grism, while additional VLTI developments continue expanding operational capabilities.

Items.Authors: Dominic F. Sanchez, Philip Hinz, Mark Chun, Daren Dillon, Elinor Gates, Christopher Ratliff, Charlotte Z. Bond
Items.Title: First on-sky demonstration of a three-sided reflective pyramid wavefront sensor with ShaneAO
Items.Abstract: We present the first on-sky closed-loop adaptive optics correction using a three-sided reflective pyramid wavefront sensor (3RPWFS) on the Shane Telescope at Lick Observatory. The 3RPWFS was operated in closed loop on bright natural guide stars and directly compared to the facility Shack–Hartmann wavefront sensor, achieving comparable Strehl performance with differences within ~10% after software reinitialization. The sensor uses a reflective three-facet pyramid with transmissive wedge modulation operated at 100 Hz. Reduced throughput from uncoated prototype optics limits faint-star performance, and control sensitivity to gain and bleed parameters was observed. This first on-sky demonstration suggests that an optimized 3RPWFS is a viable broadband alternative to conventional pyramid sensors.

Items.Authors: Philip M. Hinz, Mark Chun
Items.Title: Slumped shell-based mirrors and telescopes
Items.Abstract: Astronomical mirrors are traditionally fabricated by grinding and polishing thick, low-expansion glass substrates—a costly, tedious process. Float glass for non-optical uses is smooth and flat but much cheaper. If float glass could be shaped correctly, it could bypass the expensive grind-and-polish process.  We report progress making 0.3-1.5 m curved optics suitable for telescopes, currently for adaptive secondary mirrors. However, these sizes suit primary mirror segments as well. The slumping process can create off-axis segments that traditionally require stressed-mirror polishing. Actuators, drive electronics, and integrated position sensors maintain shape, replacing stiff glass structures.   This paper outlines using such segments to create fast (f/1 or faster), large aperture, lightweight telescopes in compact enclosures. We describe a 4-5 m prototype around a 5 m ROC primary with seven segments, and a 20 m aperture design fitting a Keck-like dome.

Items.Authors: Dennis M. Egan
Items.Title: Conquering wear plate cracking on the 100 meter Green Bank Telescope
Items.Abstract: The Green Bank Telescope azimuth track has been plagued by wear plate cracking issues since it went into service. At $30K for each plate this is a major maintenance cost with as much as a year lead time. Following an extensive numerical analysis project the track was redesigned and replaced in 2007. Some aspects of track behavior were improved but wear plate cracking continued albeit with different characteristics than before still necessitating the replacement of 6 to 10 plates each year. In 2017 a peening program was applied to the plates with some minor improvement. In 2022, using the observed plate crack behavior and revisiting some questionable results in the original numerical analysis, changes were made in the wear plate bolting configuration to improve clamping forces. Three years into the new regime track life records indicate that there is a significant improvement in wear plate life.

Items.Authors: Yashvi Sharma, Dan Weatherill
Items.Title: Eregion: a flexible framework for detector characterization tasks
Items.Abstract: Characterizing imaging detectors is essential in astronomical instrumentation and requires diverse preprocessing and analysis tasks with multiple possible techniques. While some algorithms can be reused, many tasks are unique to specific detector types, yet existing pipelines remain rigid, project-specific, and difficult to adapt across detectors and facilities. We present Eregion—a flexible, extensible software framework for detector characterization across CCDs, CMOS-APS, HgCdTe hybrid arrays, and lm-APD arrays. It provides reusable core functions wrapped in modular nodes that may be combined into workflows or used interactively, with optional streaming modes for real-time analysis during testing. Customizable data models support detector-specific properties, and a lightweight plugin system enables integration of new tasks without altering the core, facilitating collaborative development across teams.

Items.Title: First light of HARPS3 at the Isaac Newton Telescope
Items.Abstract: The High Accuracy Radial velocity Planet Searcher 3 (HARPS3), is a stabilised high-resolution spectrograph designed and built to undertake the Terra Hunting Experiment – a 10 year survey to collect nightly observations of the brightest solar-like stars in an endeavour to detect low-mass, long-period exoplanets akin to our own Earth. HARPS3 was installed and commissioned on the newly roboticised 2.54 m Isaac Newton Telescope (INT) in La Palma over the course of Winter-Spring 2026. Here we present the first-light results of HARPS3 and report on the key as-measured system parameters – spectral format and resolution, efficiency, and short-term RV stability. We will also present a general system description, with the aim to highlight the verified performances of the various sub-systems. We provide an update on the status of the longer timescale tests and the functionality of the robotic operation. Open-time observations using HARPS3 will be available through the ING for the 2026B semester.

Items.Authors: Marcos A. van Dam, Mahawa Cisse, Antonin H. Bouchez
Items.Title: On-sky demonstration of segment piston estimation using an infrared tip-tilt sensor
Items.Abstract: The Laser Tomography Adaptive Optics system for the GMT uses six Shack-Hartmann Wavefront Sensors (SHWFSs) guiding on six laser guide stars to measure high-order wavefront aberrations. Tip-tilt aberrations are affected by the disturbances in the uplink, so are measured with a natural star using an infrared tip-tilt sensor at 500 Hz. Segment piston is invisible to the SHWFSs. Simulations show that segment piston can be extracted from tip-tilt sensor measurements using phase retrieval algorithms. Several on-sky experiments were performed at the W.M. Keck Observatory to verify the performance of these algorithms. To emulate the large segments of the GMT, the Keck primary mirror was divided into 3 blocks of 12 segments, with different values of piston were applied to each block. Adaptive optics corrected short exposure images were used to recover segment piston. The experiments confirm the suitability of phase retrieval to maintain telescope phasing for the GMT.

Items.Authors: Elizabeth M. George, Domingo Alvarez Mendez, Nagaraja Naidu Bezawada, Derek J. Ives, Mark Neeser, Benoit Serra
Items.Title: Persistence characteristics of H4RG-15 detectors for ESO instruments
Items.Abstract: As a part of the ESO Instrumentation Program, we already procured 23 H4RG-15 (2.5 um cut-off) detectors for the instruments MOONS, MICADO, and HARMONI, with more of these detectors planned for future instruments on the VLT and ELT. As part of our comprehensive detector testing program, we characterize detector persistence at temperatures between 40 and 85 K, allowing the best-informed choice of operating temperature for the science focal planes. We report the characteristics of persistence as a function of temperature for the 5 MOONS detectors and 9 MICADO detectors that have already been tested between 2019 and 2025. These detectors show a rich variety of persistence behaviour that can be explained with a few different trapping and decay models. We produce persistence trap maps and a model for persistence decay for each device, allowing automatic pipeline correction of persistence and also simulation of persistence behaviour of individual detectors using the PyXel detector simulator.

Items.Title: Status of the PLATO mission cameras: final TVAC results and performance summary for the flight models
Items.Abstract: PLATO is the M3 class ESA mission dedicated to the discovery and study of extrasolar planetary systems through the detection of planetary transits. The PLATO Payload Camera units are integrated and vibrated at CSL and then TVAC tested for thermal acceptance and performance verification at SRON, IAS and INTA. Fifteen of the twenty six Flight Cameras were delivered to ESA between June 2023 and June 2024. The remaining eleven Flight Cameras and three Flight Spares, two of which completed TVAC testing, were subsequently integrated and verified, completing the campaign.    This paper provides an update following the end of the full camera test programme, with a focus on the later series models. Representative performance results and an overview of the integration and verification flow are presented, together with a final status of the camera population and key observations from carrying out a serial production style test campaign.

Items.Authors: Dmitry V. Vorobiev, Brian Fleming, Kevin France, Thomas Patton
Items.Title: The MAGPIE mission: an integral field spectroscopic UV survey of the local universe in the 2030's
Items.Abstract: MAGPIE is a smallsat mission to study the drivers of star formation and stellar feedback in the local universe, by performing several spectroscopic surveys in parts of the Milky Way, the galactic neighborhood, and galaxies at redshift z~0.01. MAGPIE is designed to study these objects in the rest frame UV range of 100 – 205 nm with high efficiency, using a 35 cm aperture telescope, an image slicer, high efficiency optical coatings, aberration-corrected diffraction gratings, low background detectors, and a cascading spectrograph design. The MAGPIE IFS delivers a spectral resolution of R~3400 and spatial resolution of ~7 arcseconds, over an instantaneous field of view of 1.25 x 6.5 arcminutes. MAGPIE's resolution, field of view, and sensitivity to faint, diffuse gas are designed to be complimentary to the UV missions of the 2030s, including ULTRASAT, HST, and UVEX.

Items.Authors: Cheryl Chan, Jebum Choi, Ady James, Craig Smith, Colin Hall, Kamil Zuber, Philip Stephenson
Items.Title: Optical characterisation of an additively manufactured freeform optical system
Items.Abstract: The increasing demand for high-performance, low size, weight, and power payloads has driven the need for advanced optical systems that can deliver superior imaging capabilities within mass and volume constraints. Small sensor payloads can benefit from the image quality of freeform optical designs in its ability to correct for higher-order aberrations in compact, off-axis configurations, while maintaining high-sensitivity, high-resolution and wide field-of-view. As part of the iLAuNCH Hub Space Trailblazer program, this collaborative project pioneers the use of additive manufacturing in the fabrication of the freeform mirrors, developing the processing techniques and materials that enable enhanced control over surface form and finish. This paper presents an exemplar freeform optical system with additively manufactured optical elements, assessing the relationship between the surface metrology of individual optical elements, with the image quality achieved by the system.

Items.Authors: Rafael M. Salgueiro, Pierre Jouve, Sylvain Oberti, Yoshito H. Ono, Masayuki Akiyama, Cédric Taïssir Heritier, Benoît Neichel, Carlos M. Correia, Jesse Cranney, François Leroux, Jon Lawrence, Thierry Fusco
Items.Title: On-sky demonstration of super resolution at the VLT and Subaru
Items.Abstract: Oberti et al. (2022) have recently examined configurations in which the wavefront sensors (WFSs), namely Shack-Hartmann (SH) sensors, are deliberately offset, thereby enhancing the effective spatial sampling of the wavefront. This methodology is known as super-resolution (SR). Although the benefits of super-resolution (SR) in adaptive optics (AO) have been demonstrated numerically, an on-sky validation was still missing. We explore the SR gains from on-sky tests at VLT and Subaru, as well as from their end-to-end simulation counterparts. We show that SR allows reconstructing spatial frequencies at or above the native SH Nyquist–Shannon limit and increases the system’s frequency sensitivity. These on-sky results represent an important proof of concept for a technique that is expected to be widely used in current and future tomographic AO systems of most 8-10 meter, and future 30-40 meter class ground-based telescopes.

Items.Authors: Jade A. Yeung, Tyrone E. Woods, Patrick Côté, John Pazder
Items.Title: An exposure time calculator for the CASTOR mission's UV Multi-Object Spectrograph
Items.Abstract: The Cosmological Advanced Survey Telescope for Optical and UV Research (CASTOR) is a proposed 1 meter space telescope under development by the National Research Council of Canada, the Canadian Space Agency, and partner institutions around the world. It will serve as a successor to the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) at short wavelengths, providing continued access to the ultra-violet (UV) and blue-optical at high spatial resolution (~0.15”) over a field of view ~100x larger than HST. The UV Multi-Object Spectrograph (UVMOS) is a medium resolution (R~1500) spectrograph based on the BATMAN spectrometer that is proposed as a parallel instrument onboard CASTOR. Here we present a pixel-based, user-friendly, extensible exposure time calculator (ETC) for the CASTOR UVMOS instrument, adaptable for other space-borne MOS missions, as well as illustrative science cases outlining the unique capabilities offered by CASTOR UVMOS in the next decade.

Items.Authors: Casper Farret Jentink, Francesco Pepe, Christophe Lovis, Vincent Bourrier, René Doyon, Romain Allart, Marc Ferrari, Yann Carteret, François Wildi, Gilles Simond, Michaël Sordet, Sébastien Bovay, François Cochard
Items.Title: First light of NIGHT at the OHP 152cm Telescope
Items.Abstract: NIGHT is the first high-resolution spectrograph dedicated to surveying exoplanetary atmospheres through near-infrared helium triplet spectroscopy. Metastable helium provides a sensitive probe of atmospheric mass loss processes shaping the exoplanet population. By focusing exclusively on this science case, NIGHT employs a custom high-efficiency volume phase holographic grating, achieving 90% throughput, enabling competitive science with smaller-class telescopes. This makes NIGHT the first instrument capable of conducting large-scale exoplanet atmospheric surveys without requiring large facilities. From August 2025 to March 2026, NIGHT was installed on the 152cm telescope at Observatoire de Haute-Provence. We present first light results, including achieved resolving power (R~75,000), on-sky sensitivity, and initial transit observations. We demonstrate NIGHT's capability to characterize atmospheric escape across diverse planet types and stellar hosts, and outline the path forward.

Items.Authors: Dan Avner, Monika Soraisam, Bill Vacca, Bryan Miller, Andrew Stephens
Items.Title: GOATS: A Gemini end-to-end platform for time-domain and multi-messenger follow-up
Items.Abstract: Rapid response is essential for time-domain and multi-messenger astronomy, yet the follow-up ecosystem (alert brokers, triggering systems, reduction pipelines, and analysis tools) remains fragmented. GOATS, the Gemini Observation and Analysis of Targets System, provides a unified platform that allows astronomers to move from an alert to calibrated data products within a single web application. GOATS integrates target ingestion, Target-of-Opportunity submission and triggering of Gemini Observatory, automated data retrieval, real-time reduction through a web interface, and lightweight analysis tools. By bringing these steps together, GOATS lowers the entry barrier to rapid follow-up and prepares Gemini for the high-volume time-domain era ushered in by Rubin Observatory alerts.

Items.Authors: Pascal Huguet-Chantome, Vincent Lapere, Johannes Veyron, Julien Marque
Items.Title: Status and progress of slicer design and manufacturing at Bertin Winlight
Items.Abstract: Integral field spectrographs rely on Integral Field Units (IFUs) to reformat incoming light into rectangular patterns using optical slicers. Over the past two decades, Bertin Winlight has played a key role in the design and manufacturing of numerous glass slicers, delivering several tens of units for advanced astronomical instruments. In this paper, we discuss the main constraints associated with the production of such components, including limitations related to slice thickness, geometry, surface quality, and optical coatings. These challenges will be illustrated through recent achievements and ongoing projects, highlighting both technological progress and current manufacturing capabilities.

Items.Authors: Jian Ge, Hui Zhang, Yongshuai Zhang, Hongping Deng, Wen Chen, Kun Chen, Yingquan Yang, Yonghe Chen, Feng Dong, Wei Gao, Zongxi Song, Hongfei Zhang, Jian Wang, Lin Wen, Lianguo Wang, Weicheng Zang, Hongjing Yang, Rafael Luque, Enric Palle
Items.Title: The Earth 2.0 Space mission and its current status
Items.Abstract: The Earth 2.0 (ET) mission in China aims to detect over 4,000 Earth-sized planets, including potentially habitable Earth-sized planets around solar-type stars. ET consists of six 28-cm transit telescopes with 550 deg² fields of view and one 35-cm microlensing telescope with a 4 deg² field of view. The transit survey will observe a 550 square degree field centered on the original Kepler field, while the microlensing telescope will monitor the Galactic bulge from an Earth–Sun L2 orbit. The mission will conduct continuous monitoring for four years with a daily downlink data rate of 2,500 Gb. Mission progress will be reported.

Items.Authors: Naidu Bezawada, Derek Ives, Elizabeth George, Benoit Serra, Domingo Alvarez, Mark Farris, Anders Petersen, Majid Zandian, Liz Corrales
Items.Title: The MICADO first light imager for ELT: Detector effects and performance overview of H4RG-15 science detectors
Items.Abstract: MICADO, a Multi-Conjugated AO Imaging Camera for Deep Observations, is one of the first-light instruments for the ELT and is currently in the integration and testing phase. MICADO focal plane uses nine H4RG-15, 2.5um detectors in a close butted 3x3 mosaic. All nine science detectors have been characterised at both 85K and 40K. Teledyne has successfully eliminated the output buffer glow on the earlier H4RG-15 devices, in their latest detectors with an upgraded ROIC. Whilst most detectors show excellent performance, there are some specific detector effects observed on some during characterisation. This paper presents, a few detector effects and their behaviour with temperature, an overview of key performance metrics of all nine detectors at 85K and 40K. Persistence characteristics as a function of temperature and a special read mode as a measure of persistence mitigation from super saturated objects will also be presented.

Items.Authors: Aleksej Kiselev, Konstantinos Giannouloudis, Arne Petersen, Hauke Gerhard Hitzmann, Dennis AK
Items.Title: Toward sustainable telescope motion: supercapacitor-based energy recovery for CTA South Large Size Telescopes
Items.Abstract: The Large Size Telescopes (LST) at the Cherenkov Telescope Array South require extremely fast slewing, which leads to short but very high power peaks of up to 500 kW, while normal operation needs only a small fraction of that. Designing the grid connection for these rare peaks is inefficient. Building on earlier conceptual work, this paper applies a supercapacitor-based energy recovery system to the CTA South LST drives. The system supplies peak power during acceleration and recuperates braking energy during deceleration. A hardware-in-the-loop setup with real telescope motors, inverters, and a supercapacitor module provides the first experimental validation, demonstrating effective peak-load shaving and energy recovery for more sustainable telescope operation.

Items.Authors: Maïssa Salama, Mahawa Cissé, Rebecca Jensen-Clem, Vincent Chambouleyron, J. Kent Wallace, Mitchell Troy, Laurent Pueyo, Antonin Bouchez, Charlotte Guthery, Daniel Echeverri, Jerry Xuan, Nemanja Jovanovic, Dimitri Mawet
Items.Title: Keck Observatory as an HWO testbed: validating wavefront sensing and control techniques on a segmented telescope with a Zernike wavefront sensor for high-contrast imaging
Items.Abstract: Directly imaging a rocky planet in the habitable zone of its host star requires 10^-8 - 10^-10 contrasts. This will be the goal of the extremely large telescopes (ELTs) and the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) space mission, which will all have segmented primary mirrors. A key technical challenge is maintaining wavefront stability in the presence of segment misalignments, which add aberrations particularly damaging to contrast. Keck is currently the only telescope with a segmented primary mirror, edge sensors, deformable mirror (DM), Zernike wavefront sensor (ZWFS), and high-contrast science instruments. We are using the unique parallels between Keck and HWO architectures to validate wavefront sensing and control schemes on a segmented telescope. We report on-sky progress in implementing dual-mirror control, controlling both primary mirror segments and DM, using the ZWFS. We also compare different segment co-phasing techniques and measure their impact on NIRC2 high-contrast data.
